events.text:
Ukraine hit Russia's Novorossiysk naval base — the Black Sea Fleet's main remaining port — with a combined drone and missile strike overnight.
The confirmed damage list is significant.
The General Staff says three warships hit (minesweeper Zheleznyakov, Kalibr-carrying frigate Admiral Essen, and landing ship Pyotr Morgunov) plus fuel storage. 
Ukrainian intelligence and OSINT add frigate Admiral Makarov, a Buyan-M missile ship (assessed inoperable), patrol ship Vasily Bykov, several missile boats, and two air defense radars near Gelendzhik. 
Ukraine says a domestically built Neptune anti-ship missile hit Admiral Essen. 
Separately, Ukraine struck Makhachkala port on the Caspian — a key Russia-Iran logistics hub. 
Zelensky said Ukrainian forces hit eight Russian infrastructure sites "from the Arctic to the Caspian" in the same period. 
Satellite imagery from Exilenova+ shows fires and damage consistent with the claims. 
This is the deepest sustained pressure on Russia's Black Sea Fleet since Ukraine forced the partial evacuation of Sevastopol.

Polish PM Tusk said he received a "fairly precise" CIA briefing from Director Ratcliffe on what's coming in the months ahead, and revealed that Polish and Ukrainian services jointly averted a direct threat to a Poland-Ukraine border crossing overnight. 
He didn't specify the crossing or threat type. 
This came a day after Russian drones hit the Ukraine-Moldova border crossing at Starokozache, killing two.
Tusk said Poland should expect similar provocations and that Russia is systematically targeting border infrastructure to weaken Ukraine economically. 
CIA Director Ratcliffe had visited Moscow and met Russian intelligence leadership in late August before briefing Poland's security coordinator.

events.text:
🇮🇷 Iran doesn’t have to sink a carrier to torpedo US war effort – a bloody nose would be enough
 
The IRGC debuted its new Qasem Bassir long-range anti-ship ballistic missile last Saturday in a “combat test” targeting the US Navy’s defensive capabilities in real wartime conditions. The attack targeted the USS George Washington and a guided-missile destroyer.
IRGC talk of live “combat testing” on US vessels should send chills up CENTCOM planners’ spines. The last such “tests” (Operations True Promise I through III) saw Iran inflict incremental amounts of pain on their enemies, methodically mapping out targets and defenses, and using increasingly [sophisticated weapons and tactics.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/59557)
 
🤔 Can Iran sink a carrier?
 
Sinking a modern supercarrier is exceptionally difficult. In 2005, the Navy spent nearly a month trying to sink the decommissioned USS America using conventional weaponry, from JDAMs and Mavericks to Harpoon anti-ship missiles and Mark 48 torpedoes. After that failed, engineers had to mount explosive charges in and around the ship to finally sink the hull.
Strikes involving one or more Qasem Bassir, Abu Mahdi, or even Fattah-2 missiles probably won’t be enough to send a US carrier to the bottom of the sea, but they don’t have to:
 
🔴 Carriers are the US’s ultimate power projection tool: significant damage to their flight deck, aircraft complement, elevators, catapults, or arresting equipment would be enough to put them out of action.
🔴 The warships are extremely finnicky. This spring, a massive laundry room fire and clogged pipes ultimately forced the USS Gerald Ford to quit the fight against Iran.
🔴 Only 2-3 of the Navy’s 11 ship carrier fleet are deployed at any one time, with 1-2 more available in an emergency. The rest are undergoing routine or deep maintenance, repairs and training. The US has already deployed four carriers in the 2026 war (Lincoln, Ford, Bush, Washington) and preparing a fifth (USS Roosevelt) to replace the Washington, stretching deployments beyond their absolute limits.
➡️ USS Stennis and Truman: in the middle of a multi-year overhaul. Unusable
➡️ USS Ford: stuck in structural repairs and deep resupply until at least mid-2027
➡️ USS Eisenhower, Vinson and Reagan: lack certification and airwings for immediate deployment
➡️ USS Nimitz: preparing for decommissioning and replacement by the new USS John F. Kennedy (whose commissioning has been delayed)
 
This means if Iran successfully strikes even one of the carriers arrayed against it – slamming a missile or heavy drone into a flight deck, detonating aircraft, fuel or weaponry, or triggering a chain reaction that reaches deep into the ship’s belly, it would be enough to put it out of action [until the end of the war.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72904)
The carrier would instantly turn from a force multiplier into a burden – forcing the rest of its strike group, and other ships in CENTCOM’s AOR, to come to its aid, and effectively crippling US offensive operations. Any other carrier groups would likely pull back from Iran to avoid targeting.
With American bases in the Persian Gulf on fire, the carrier would have to limp to Diego Garcia, Oman, Souda Bay or Singapore for immediate repairs, or Yokosuka, Washington State or Virginia for a deep overhaul.
 
Maybe Iran hasn’t taken a carrier out of action yet is because they’re master diplomats, reserving the option [for the next step up the escalation ladder? ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74049)

🏆Houthis just seized historic crown jewel of Yemen’s Red Sea ports: here’s what happens next
 
In the list of vital strategic locations controlled by Yemen’s Gulf-backed puppet government, the Red Sea port city of Mokha ranked comfortably in the top three.
📍 Serving as the historic crown jewel of Yemeni ports, Mokha is a UNESCO World Heritage List contender, the birthplace of modern coffee culture, and a geostrategic prize situated just ~60-80 km from Bab al-Mandab Strait.
🌏 The Houthis shattered the stronghold’s defenses in a week, launching a rapid, coordinated ground offensive September 3, surrounding the city and cutting off enemy logistics and reinforcement routes, and entering Mokha proper on September 10. Ahead of the advance, fighters spent much of August bombarding key port targets, crippling its operations.
🌏 Before the rout began, Mocha’s defenses were considered among the most elite, disciplined and well-equipped anti-Houthi units in all of Yemen, with National Resistance Forces commander Tareq Saleh’s forces paid directly by Gulf monarchies, and armed with tanks, howitzers and anti-missile batteries.
🌏 Other anti-Houthi factions in the area included the Giants Brigades, the Taiz Military Axis, Tihama Resistance tribesmen and Nation’s Shield Forces. Together, these forces, numbering up to ~50k men, were supposed to hold out indefinitely. Instead, they crumbled in days. Saleh was forced to beat a hasty retreat, and reports suggest up to three full brigades, complete with equipment, have surrendered.
 
What Mokha’s liberation means
➡️ the city’s capture puts Houthi artillery and shorter-range drones within striking distance of Bab el-Mandeb, meaning they no longer have to use costlier missiles and UAVs to target Saudi shipping in and around the strait
➡️ the seizure deprives defenders in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, of their main logistics artery, leaving them semi-isolated and vulnerable to Houthi encirclement
➡️ Mokha in Houthi hands cripples the puppet government’s ability to disrupt Sanaa’s modest foreign resupply corridors
➡️ perhaps most importantly, it gives the Houthis a staging area for attacks on nearby strategic islands, including Perim and the Hanish Archipelago. Media report that the fighters have already captured the archipelago island of Zuqar in a coordinated attack involving ballistic and rocket attacks and speedboats
➡️ with Mokha secured, the Houthis are now a ~45 km drive south to Dhubab – the absolute last Red Sea coastal town still in control of enemy forces
🤔 It’s all beginning to look a lot like Afghanistan, circa August 2021.
